content.value_statement: Teams often overbuild while trying to make failing tests pass. This skill guides Claude, Codex, and Claude Code toward minimal green-phase implementation.
actual_capabilities: Guides review of failing tests and error messages before implementation.
Prompts minimal code changes that satisfy the next failing test.
Encourages running tests after each change to confirm progress.
Documents shortcuts and technical debt for the later refactor phase.
Provides language and framework examples for common green-phase patterns.
limitations: It does not replace project-specific test judgment or code review.
It is not intended for broad refactoring or architecture redesign.
It depends on available failing tests to define required behavior.
It may defer validation, error handling, or performance work until refactoring.

use_cases.title: Make a failing unit test pass
use_cases.description: Use the workflow to identify the smallest implementation that satisfies one failing test.

use_cases.title: Guide a team TDD session
use_cases.description: Keep pair programming or mob programming focused on green-phase constraints and clear debt notes.

use_cases.title: Review agent-generated fixes
use_cases.description: Check that an AI coding agent changed only what the failing tests required.

prompt_templates.title: Pass one failing test
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this TDD green workflow on the failing test I provide. Implement the smallest behavior needed, run the test, and list any shortcut.

prompt_templates.title: Handle a feature slice
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these failing tests and implement only the required feature slice. Run the relevant tests after each change and summarize remaining debt.

prompt_templates.title: Constrain an AI coding agent
prompt_templates.prompt: Apply the green-phase rules to this repository. Avoid refactoring, avoid extra behavior, and report each minimal change with its passing test evidence.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare for refactor phase
prompt_templates.prompt: After making the failing tests pass, produce a readiness note. Include shortcuts, duplicated logic, missing validation, and recommended refactor targets.

output_examples.input: A failing user creation test expects a saved user id and matching email.
output_examples.output: The response identifies the smallest storage change, confirms the target test passes, and records database integration as refactor-phase debt.

output_examples.input: An API test expects a created task response with status 201.
output_examples.output: The response proposes an in-memory handler, runs the route test, and avoids adding validation not required by the test.

output_examples.input: Several model tests fail around product price validation.
output_examples.output: The response implements only the required validation rule, verifies the failing tests are green, and lists broader model cleanup for later.

best_practices: Start with the simplest failing test and make one observable behavior pass.
Run the relevant test after each change and keep the feedback loop short.
Record every shortcut so the refactor phase has clear targets.
anti_patterns: Do not add features that are not required by a failing test.
Do not refactor while the code is still red.
Do not bypass or weaken tests to create a false green state.

faq.question: What is the TDD green phase?
faq.answer: It is the step where you write the smallest implementation needed to make a failing test pass.

faq.question: Does this skill write production-ready code?
faq.answer: It prioritizes passing tests first. Production hardening is usually saved for the refactor phase.

faq.question: Can I use it with Claude, Codex, and Claude Code?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill is written for AI coding agents that can inspect tests, edit code, and run test commands.

faq.question: Should I add new tests while using this skill?
faq.answer: No. Add or revise tests during the red phase, then use this skill to make those tests pass.

faq.question: How does it handle technical debt?
faq.answer: It records shortcuts, missing validation, and simple implementations so the next refactor step is clear.

faq.question: When should I avoid this skill?
faq.answer: Avoid it when tests already pass, when you need architecture work, or when the task is mainly performance tuning.
